sections.overview: The western flower thrips is a tiny, highly polyphagous insect native to North America and now established in many world regions.
sections.identification: Adults are about a millimetre long; under magnification, eight antennal segments distinguish it from the similar onion thrips, which has seven.
sections.habitat: It occupies flowers and growing tissues on a very broad range of wild, vegetable and ornamental hosts, including greenhouse crops.
sections.diet: Both larvae and adults feed on plant tissues, pollen and flowers; females and nymphs may also eat mite eggs when available.
sections.behavior: Adults and larvae remain active when conditions are warm; in greenhouses, individuals shelter in protected sites during cold periods.
sections.reproduction: Females insert eggs into plant tissue, and reproduction may be sexual or asexual; later immature stages usually pupate in the substrate.
sections.ecology: Feeding scars can deform leaves, flowers and fruit, and the thrips efficiently transmits several plant viruses between hosts.
sections.conservation: It is an important crop pest and virus vector rather than a species evaluated for wildlife conservation; its distribution reflects global plant trade.
